prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The five frames show a close laboratory bench: the camera wearer’s gloved hands and forearms are nearest, roughly 0.2–0.6 m away, while tube racks, pipettes, boxes, bottles, and an ice-filled black tray lie across the bench at about 0.5–1.2 m; cabinets and rear-bench equipment are farther away, roughly 1–2 m. The bright arms reveal their reach across the front of the body, and the tray and nearby racks remain within arm’s reach; no separate person is clearly resolved. Across the frames, the hands move from the lower-left/front toward the centre and then the upper-centre/right, while the tray shifts from right-of-centre to centre and back toward the right as the head turns. The depth map makes near/far ordering and occlusion by the arms clearer than RGB, but its monocular scale is uncertain, object boundaries bleed together, and several reflective, dark, or partly cropped regions have implausible depths.
descriptions.segmentation: The masks separate some spatially distinct regions on the bench, including several small upright containers along the rear edge, larger central objects, and the camera wearer’s partially cropped arms entering from the lower or side borders. Their positions track the head turn: masked objects slide horizontally across frames, and the large arm/hand region expands into the centre-right by the final frames, occluding parts of the bench. The map can make silhouettes and overlap order easier to see than RGB, especially for foreground arms against clustered equipment, but it does not provide metric distance or reliable facing direction. It is highly unreliable here: many laboratory items are mislabeled as pizza, cake, TV, keyboard, book, remote, dining table, or bottle, broad background areas merge into single masks, and person masks inconsistently cover the camera wearer’s arms; no other person or gaze direction can be established.
descriptions.pose: The pose strip is entirely black in all five frames, so it supplies no detected body, hand skeleton, joint locations, facing direction, gaze direction, reach estimate, or temporal motion. It therefore adds no spatial information beyond the RGB and cannot distinguish the camera wearer’s visible gloved hands from any other person. The RGB shows the wearer’s arms entering from the lower-left or lower-centre and extending toward the bench, but none of those limbs is represented in this map. For this sequence the pose output is a complete detection failure, likely affected by the egocentric viewpoint, close cropping, gloves, sleeves, and frequent partial visibility.
